+# Related problems and where compute actually binds
+
+Each heading names one concrete option from framer.md, with which part of the root question it bears on, whether more parallel compute changes its answer (open / settled / none), and the sequential structure of one answer.
+
+## Multiple shooting
+
+The root question's scheme verbatim: guess the trajectory at every grid point, integrate each sub-interval from its guessed value in parallel, then force continuity with a Newton iteration (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_multiple_shooting_method).
+
+- **Root link:** Q1 — whether a single long sequential simulation can be parallelised over time by guessing the whole trajectory and Newton-correcting every step at once.
+- **Compute:** none (convergence is set by the Newton iteration, not by how many processors evaluate segments).
+- **Sequential:** one answer is one trajectory needing k Newton iterations, each a forward substitution in which interval t's correction waits on interval t-1 (O(m) deep for m intervals), while the m segment integrations are independent and parallelise exactly; the correction chain is the only serial residue because J is block lower-bidiagonal (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/parareal.pdf).
+
+## Parareal
+
+The cheap-Jacobian realisation of multiple shooting, introduced by Lions, Maday and Turinici: a coarse serial propagator predicts the trajectory and fine integrators correct each interval in parallel, iterating to convergence (https://parallel-in-time.org/methods/parareal.html).
+
+- **Root link:** Q2 — whether the guess+Newton-correct trick only works when the system forgets its past — and Q1.
+- **Compute:** none (the iteration count k is set by the forgetting rate, not the hardware).
+- **Sequential:** each iteration marches a coarse propagator serially over all T subintervals (step t waits on t-1) while the T fine integrations are independent, so one run's depth is k·T, with k set by the forward decay of the coarse-guess error — Gander and Hairer show superlinear convergence only for contractive systems (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/gander_plenary2007.pdf).
+
+## MGRIT
+
+The non-intrusive multigrid-reduction-in-time version of Parareal (shipped as XBraid), which coarsens the time grid rather than using a separate coarse model (https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).
+
+- **Root link:** Q3 — whether compute is a blocker and could be fixed with massive GPU parallelism.
+- **Compute:** settled — for parabolic (dissipative) PDEs MGRIT is demonstrated to be an optimal-scaling solver, and LLNL reports "tenfold or more" time-to-solution drops for compressible Navier-Stokes, so more parallel compute already pays off there (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1184744; https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).
+- **Sequential:** one run keeps the same coarse/fine structure as Parareal — a coarse-grid correction sweeps the time levels in order while fine-grid integrations are independent — and the iteration count is set by the contraction (forgetting) rate, not processor count, so the causal coarse sweep cannot be reordered without cyclic reduction (https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).
+
+## ParaDiag / ParaExp
+
+Direct time-parallel methods for linear dynamics: x_T = A^T x_0 is computed by diagonalisation or repeated squaring in O(log T) depth, giving exact parallel-in-time with no forgetting assumption (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/siamtoc3.php).
+
+- **Root link:** Q2's exception — the one regime where the causality principle can be cleanly side-stepped — and Q1.
+- **Compute:** none.
+- **Sequential:** none — the T sequential steps already collapse because the propagator A^T can be composed out of order by repeated squaring/diagonalisation in O(log T) parallel steps (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/siamtoc3.php).
+
+## Cyclic reduction (PCR)
+
+Parallel cyclic reduction solves the block-bidiagonal Newton correction (a tridiagonal/bidiagonal system) in O(log N) steps with N-fold parallelism, dropping the per-iteration depth of the PinT methods from O(T) to O(log T) (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs554/fa2015/notes/09_tridiagonal_8up.pdf).
+
+- **Root link:** Q3 — the "shit ton of GPU parallelism" question — specifically whether width can shorten the cheap sequential part.
+- **Compute:** settled — N-fold parallel cyclic reduction is known to solve a tridiagonal system in O(log N) steps instead of O(N), so more parallel compute already buys the O(T)→O(log T) per-iteration depth reduction (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs554/fa2015/notes/09_tridiagonal_8up.pdf).
+- **Sequential:** the block-bidiagonal solve is a forward substitution in which row t waits on row t-1 (O(T) deep per iteration), but the rows need not run in order: cyclic reduction eliminates independent pairs simultaneously, which pays off only when the T equations can be halved each round and the machine has ~T processors to feed them (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs554/fa2015/notes/09_tridiagonal_8up.pdf).
+
+## Speculative prefetching
+
+The MCMC analog of guess+correct: speculatively evaluate many possible accept/reject branches in parallel, keep the true path, discard the rest, with a speedup that is bounded and constant-factor (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf).
+
+- **Root link:** Q2 for MCMC — whether the trick only works when the system forgets — and Q3's width-versus-depth point.
+- **Compute:** none (mixing binds; prefetching only reduces latency with a bounded, constant-factor speedup).
+- **Sequential:** one MH chain is a serial accept/reject sequence (each proposal waits on the previous accepted state, T steps per run), and prefetching speculates J future branches in parallel but keeps one path, giving O(log2 J) depth with J cores and expected speedup ≈1/α ≈ 4.3 at the 0.234 acceptance rate, largest when rejection dominates (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf; https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7265).
+
+## Regeneration / splitting
+
+Splitting an MCMC sampler at regeneration times yields i.i.d. tours that can be simulated in parallel, avoiding the bias of many short independent chains (https://galton.uchicago.edu/~mykland/paperlinks/MyklandTierneyYu2291148.pdf).
+
+- **Root link:** Q2 for MCMC — regeneration is the operational "forgets its past" condition.
+- **Compute:** none.
+- **Sequential:** none — the tours between regeneration times are i.i.d. and already split into independent pieces that can run on separate processors, leaving only the mixing-governed length of one tour as the serial residue (https://galton.uchicago.edu/~mykland/paperlinks/MyklandTierneyYu2291148.pdf).
+
+## Coupling from the past
+
+Propp-Wilson exact sampling: run the chain from all possible states simultaneously under a monotone coupling, and coalescence certifies an exact draw, efficient only when coalescence (mixing) is fast (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/206-RWG/RWGpapers/propp_wilson.pdf).
+
+- **Root link:** Q2 for MCMC — coalescence is the "forgets its past" condition.
+- **Compute:** none.
+- **Sequential:** none — the coupled chains run from all states in parallel under one monotone update, so the work already splits across states, and the only serial quantity is the coalescence time, which is set by mixing, not compute (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/206-RWG/RWGpapers/propp_wilson.pdf).
+
+## Many-chain / data-parallel sampling (TFP HMC)
+
+GPUs/TPUs add width two ways — many chains at once and data-parallel gradient/log-density evaluation within one chain — but width does not shorten a single chain's critical path (https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2022/11/13/stan-and-tensorflow-for-fast-parallel-bayesian-inference/).
+
+- **Root link:** Q3 — the GPU question — specifically the width-versus-depth distinction.
+- **Compute:** open — the quantity more parallel compute would buy is the number of independent chains/seeds analysed: Angelino et al. show running many chains "does not change the mixing time for any single chain" (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf), and no cited source establishes whether adding more chains/seeds above that changes the posterior estimate (e.g. finds additional modes).
+- **Sequential:** none — many chains and within-chain data-parallel likelihoods are already independent pieces, so the answer already splits across GPUs, and the per-chain critical path (T × per-step cost × mixing overhead) is unchanged by width (https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2022/11/13/stan-and-tensorflow-for-fast-parallel-bayesian-inference/).
+
+## GLUE / rainfall-runoff calibration
+
+The actual compute burden in daily-step rainfall-runoff modelling is Monte-Carlo parameter calibration and GLUE uncertainty analysis, parallelised with MPI/OpenMP/CUDA across parameter sets, explicitly not across time steps (https://doi.org/10.3390/w15152810).
+
+- **Root link:** Q3 — the hydrology example showing compute is not a time-dimension blocker.
+- **Compute:** settled — the compute burden is parameter calibration/GLUE uncertainty, parallelised across parameter sets (embarrassingly parallel, never across time), so more parallel compute already buys parameter-set throughput, not time-step depth (https://doi.org/10.3390/w15152810; https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/12/10/2667).
+- **Sequential:** none — each parameter set is one cheap forward run of a lumped model and parameter sets are independent, so the work already splits into independent pieces with no serial time chain to shorten (https://doi.org/10.3390/w15152810).
+
+## Chaotic / non-forgetting PinT
+
+On chaotic systems (Lorenz, hyperbolic PDEs) the coarse-guess error is amplified forward, so Parareal diverges or its superlinear convergence stops, because chaotic initial value problems are inherently ill-conditioned (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1880928; https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441).
+
+- **Root link:** Q2 — whether the trick only works when the system forgets — here the non-forgetting failure mode.
+- **Compute:** open — the quantity more parallel compute would buy is the coarse-grid resolution or number of processors fed to the coarse propagator: published results stop at divergence ("parareal diverging in many cases", https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1880928), and whether scaling coarse-grid fidelity or iteration count changes convergence above that is unresolved (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441).
+- **Sequential:** the coarse propagator must march the time levels in order (step t waits on t-1), so one run's depth is T × k iterations, and the positive-Lyapunov amplification means the iterations cannot be collapsed by reordering the causal chain; the nearest attempt at a fix is the coarse-grid-correction study in (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441).

1: # Parallelising one long sequential simulation over time: guess, Newton-correct, and the "forgetting" condition
2: 
3: ## 0. Current understanding (relayed before answering)
4: 
5: Three questions are on the table:
6: 
7: 1. Can a single long sequential simulation — e.g. one MCMC chain, or a rainfall-runoff model stepped through decades of daily rainfall — be parallelised over time by *guessing the whole trajectory and then correcting every step at once with Newton iterations*?
8: 2. Does that trick *only* work when the system forgets its past?
9: 3. Is *compute* a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed with "a shit ton of GPU parallelism"?
10: 
11: Let me define the object precisely so the later claims are not hand-wavy.
12: 
13: **The object.** A trajectory is a sequence of states `x_t ∈ R^d` satisfying `x_{t+1} = f(x_t, u_t)` for a deterministic map `f` (the rainfall-runoff case is this, with `u_t` the daily forcing), or, for MCMC, `x_{t+1} ~ P(· | x_t)` (a stochastic transition kernel, e.g. Metropolis-Hastings). Sequential time-stepping computes `x_T` in `T` steps; each step costs `O(c)` work, giving `O(T·c)` total *work* and — the part that matters for parallelisation — `O(T)` *depth* (critical path length). The question is whether that depth can be collapsed below `O(T)`.
14: 
15: **What "guess + Newton-correct" would mean mathematically.** Guess all the states at once, `X = (x_0, ..., x_{T-1})`. Define the residual whose components are the continuity conditions `F_t(X) = x_{t+1} - f(x_t, u_t) = 0`; solving `F(X) = 0` recovers the exact trajectory. Newton's method iterates `X ← X - J^{-1} F(X)`. Two observations that will drive everything:
16: 
17: - The *residual evaluation* `F(X)` is fully parallel over `t` — this is the "guess the whole trajectory and evaluate every step at once" part, and it is exactly why the idea is attractive.
18: - The *Jacobian* `J` of a one-step map is block lower-bidiagonal (step `t` couples only to `t-1`), so the Newton correction `J^{-1}F` is a forward substitution, i.e. *sequential in `T`* — unless it is attacked with cyclic reduction (see §2.6).
19: 
20: This is not a new idea; it is the **multiple shooting** method, and **Parareal** is a cheap-Jacobian approximation of it (details and sources in §2.1).
21: 
22: **What "forgets its past" means.** For deterministic dynamics, the sensitivity of `x_{t+s}` to `x_t` is the product of Jacobians, with magnitude growing like `e^{λs}` where `λ` is the maximal Lyapunov exponent. "Forgetting" means `λ < 0` (dissipative/contractive): a perturbation at time `t` is *damped*, not amplified, as it propagates forward. For MCMC, the analogous property is **mixing** — the distribution of `x_{t+s}` becomes independent of `x_t` — or, operationally, **regeneration**: times at which the chain's future is independent of its past. In both cases "forgets its past" = long-range causal coupling decays, so a bad guess early on is washed out by the time it matters.
23: 
24: ## 1. Predictions (made before checking the literature)
25: 
26: - **P1.** The "guess + Newton-correct" proposal is real and studied: it is multiple shooting, with Parareal / MGRIT / PFASST as its practical realisations. It parallelises the *expensive* part (segment integration) while leaving a *cheap* sequential part (coarse propagation / bidiagonal Newton solve).
27: - **P2.** Fast convergence (`k ≪ T` iterations) requires the coarse-guess error to decay forward — i.e. the system must forget (negative Lyapunov exponents, dissipative, fast mixing). A memoryful or chaotic system should need `O(T)` iterations (no speedup) or diverge.
28: - **P3.** The linear case is the exception: `x_T = A^T x_0` is computable in `O(log T)` depth by repeated squaring/diagonalisation, with no forgetting assumption.
29: - **P4.** For a *single* daily rainfall-runoff run, compute is not the blocker — a forward run of a lumped conceptual model is trivially cheap; the real cost is calibration/uncertainty over *parameters*, which is embarrassingly parallel across parameters, not across time.
30: - **P5.** For a single long MCMC chain, the blocker is *mixing* (a statistical property), not FLOPs; GPUs add width (many chains, data-parallel likelihoods) but not depth (they don't shorten one chain's critical path), except via speculative prefetching, which is a branch-prediction trick with bounded speedup that is largest precisely when the chain barely moves.
31: - **P6.** "A shit ton of GPU parallelism" can reduce the cheap sequential part from `O(T)` to `O(log T)` via cyclic reduction, dropping per-iteration depth to `O(log T)`, but it cannot reduce the *number of iterations* `k`, which is set by the forgetting rate.
32: 
33: Predicted headline: the primary blocker is the system's memory/mixing, not compute — i.e. **NOT COMPUTE-BOUND** — with compute mattering only in specific subproblems.
34: 
35: ## 2. Analysis
36: 
37: ### 2.1 The method is real and well-understood
38: 
39: The proposal — guess the whole trajectory, then Newton-correct the continuity conditions — is literally **multiple shooting**. Wikipedia's statement of the method matches the question almost verbatim: partition the interval at grid points, "start by guessing the values of y at all grid points," integrate each sub-interval from its guessed initial value, and impose the matching conditions with "a modification of Newton's method" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_multiple_shooting_method).
40: 
41: The Gander–Vandewalle analysis of Parareal makes the connection explicit: multiple shooting is "to decompose the time-integration interval into subintervals, to solve an initial value problem on each subinterval concurrently, and to force continuity of the solution branches on successive intervals by means of a Newton procedure" (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/parareal.pdf). Parareal itself was introduced by Lions, Maday, and Turinici as a coarse/fine predictor-corrector in time (https://parallel-in-time.org/methods/parareal.html), and MGRIT (Falgout et al.) is the non-intrusive multigrid-reduction-in-time version shipped as XBraid (https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid; https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1184744).
42: 
43: ### 2.2 The "forgets its past" condition is essentially the enabling condition
44: 
45: This is where P2 gets tested against the record.
46: 
47: - **Contractive/dissipative systems converge fast.** Gander and Hairer prove *superlinear* convergence of Parareal for nonlinear ODEs on bounded intervals — the error after iteration `k` is `O(ΔT^{p(k+1)})/(k+1)!`-style, shrinking as `k` grows (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/gander_plenary2007.pdf). For parabolic (dissipative) PDEs, MGRIT is demonstrated to be an optimal-scaling solver (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1184744), and LLNL reports time-to-solution drops of "tenfold or more" for compressible Navier-Stokes (https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).
48: - **Chaotic / non-forgetting systems fail or degenerate.** The same Gander–Hairer paper shows that on the Lorenz equations (chaotic), the superlinear convergence "stops at a certain level" as chaos amplifies the coarse-grid discrepancy. More bluntly, LLNL's report on chaotic problems states that for hyperbolic/chaotic problems "the most common method, parareal, diverging in many cases," because "chaotic initial value problems are inherently ill-conditioned" (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1880928), and Vargas et al. open with the same point: chaos makes subtle coarse-level inaccuracies explode into bad coarse-grid corrections (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441). This is exactly the "does not forget" failure mode: a positive Lyapunov exponent means a bad guess at time `t` is amplified forward, so the Newton/coarse correction never settles.
49: 
50: So, for nonlinear systems: yes, the value of the method tracks the forgetting rate. The method *is* a way to convert "sequential-in-time" into "parallel + iterate," and the iteration count `k` is governed by how fast errors decay — a property of the dynamics, not the hardware.
51: 
52: ### 2.3 The exception: linear systems get parallel-in-time for free
53: 
54: For a linear map `x_{t+1} = A x_t`, the final state is `x_T = A^T x_0`, computable by repeated squaring in `O(log T)` depth. The "direct time parallel methods based on diagonalisation" (ParaDiag/ParaExp) exploit exactly this, solving the whole time interval at once for linear problems (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/siamtoc3.php, §5.5). No forgetting is needed — confirming P3 — because a linear propagator can be composed out of order. This is the only regime where the causality principle can be cleanly side-stepped.
55: 
56: ### 2.4 The fundamental depth limit: causality and inherent sequentiality
57: 
58: Gander's survey names the obstacle plainly: for evolution problems "there is a causality principle: the solution later in time is affected (it is even determined) by the solution earlier in time, but not the other way round" (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/50YearsTimeParallel.pdf). That is not just folklore: in complexity theory, the forward simulation of a local dynamics is a canonical example of a *probably inherently sequential* problem. The P-completeness page lists "Game of Life — given an initial configuration ... is that cell alive after T steps" among the problems that are "probably not parallelizable" / "inherently sequential" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-complete), and Greenlaw–Hoover–Ruzzo's *Limits to Parallel Computation* develops the framework: such problems appear to lack polylog-time, polynomial-processor (NC) algorithms, i.e. "applying more processors ... appears to be broken" for them (https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~ruzzo/papers/limits.pdf).
59: 
60: The consequence: there is **no general free lunch**. For arbitrary local dynamics with memory, no number of processors removes the `O(T)` causal dependence. Parallel-in-time methods work only by *exploiting structure* — contraction (Parareal/MGRIT), linearity (ParaDiag), or a coarse/fine work separation that leaves a cheap serial residue.
61: 
62: ### 2.5 The MCMC analog, and why Newton does not literally apply
63: 
64: A Metropolis-Hastings step is a stochastic accept/reject branch, not a smooth map, so there is no residual to Newton-solve. The faithful analog of "guess + correct" is **speculative prefetching**: speculatively evaluate many possible future states (the accept/reject tree) in parallel, keep the true path, discard the rest. Two recorded facts matter:
65: 
66: - Running many independent chains "does not change the mixing time for any single chain" (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf). So the embarrassingly-parallel answer does *not* reduce the sequential length that a slow-mixing chain needs.
67: - Prefetching's speedup is *bounded and constant-factor*, not a complexity win: naive prefetching gives `O(log2 J)` with `J` cores, and Byrd et al.'s "speculative moves" gives expected speedup `≈ 1/α` (about 4.3 at the optimal 0.234 acceptance rate) (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf; https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7265). Note the perverse structure: this speedup is largest when rejection dominates, i.e. when the chain is *barely moving* — the opposite of fast mixing.
68: 
69: The "forgets its past" condition for MCMC is **regeneration**. Mykland, Tierney, and Yu introduced splitting into MCMC samplers precisely so that the tours between regeneration times are i.i.d. and "allows Markov chain sampling to take advantage of a parallel computing environment without the problems created by many short Markov chain runs" (https://galton.uchicago.edu/~mykland/paperlinks/MyklandTierneyYu2291148.pdf). Coupling from the past (Propp & Wilson) parallelises the *other* way: run the chain from *all* possible states simultaneously under a monotone coupling, and coalescence certifies an exact sample — but this is efficient only when coalescence (≈ mixing) is fast (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/206-RWG/RWGpapers/propp_wilson.pdf). Both are literally "the system forgets" conditions.
70: 
71: This exposes the central tension, and it is the sharpest version of P2/P5:
72: 
73: > A single long chain is needed *only when* mixing is slow; but slow mixing is *exactly when* time-parallelism (regeneration, CFTP, prefetching) gives little or nothing.
74: 
75: If the chain mixes fast, you don't need one long chain — many short independent chains suffice, and that is embarrassingly parallel already. If it mixes slowly, the memory is what forces the long run, and that memory is what defeats time-parallel correction. So for MCMC, time-parallelism is largely self-defeating, consistent with the P-completeness intuition of §2.4.
76: 
77: ### 2.6 Is compute a major blocker? The GPU question
78: 
79: **Width versus depth.** GPUs add enormous *width* (SIMD lanes), and modern samplers use it in two ways: running many chains at once, and data-parallel gradient/log-density evaluation *within* a single chain. TensorFlow Probability's HMC "gets parallelism both within-chain (mostly from data parallelism) and across chains ... for free" on GPUs/TPUs (https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2022/11/13/stan-and-tensorflow-for-fast-parallel-bayesian-inference/; https://export.arxiv.org/pdf/2002.01184). But width does not shorten the *depth* of a single trajectory: the critical path remains `T × (per-step cost) × (mixing overhead)`. This is the Amdahl's-law-in-time point.
80: 
81: **Where massive parallelism does buy depth.** The cheap sequential part of the PinT methods — the coarse propagation / block-bidiagonal Newton solve — is a (block) tridiagonal/bidiagonal solve. # Parallelising one long sequential simulation over time: guess, Newton-correct, and the "forgetting" condition

## 0. Current understanding (relayed before answering)

Three questions are on the table:

1. Can a single long sequential simulation — e.g. one MCMC chain, or a rainfall-runoff model stepped through decades of daily rainfall — be parallelised over time by *guessing the whole trajectory and then correcting every step at once with Newton iterations*?
2. Does that trick *only* work when the system forgets its past?
3. Is *compute* a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed with "a shit ton of GPU parallelism"?

Let me define the object precisely so the later claims are not hand-wavy.

**The object.** A trajectory is a sequence of states `x_t ∈ R^d` satisfying `x_{t+1} = f(x_t, u_t)` for a deterministic map `f` (the rainfall-runoff case is this, with `u_t` the daily forcing), or, for MCMC, `x_{t+1} ~ P(· | x_t)` (a stochastic transition kernel, e.g. Metropolis-Hastings). Sequential time-stepping computes `x_T` in `T` steps; each step costs `O(c)` work, giving `O(T·c)` total *work* and — the part that matters for parallelisation — `O(T)` *depth* (critical path length). The question is whether that depth can be collapsed below `O(T)`.

**What "guess + Newton-correct" would mean mathematically.** Guess all the states at once, `X = (x_0, ..., x_{T-1})`. Define the residual whose components are the continuity conditions `F_t(X) = x_{t+1} - f(x_t, u_t) = 0`; solving `F(X) = 0` recovers the exact trajectory. Newton's method iterates `X ← X - J^{-1} F(X)`. Two observations that will drive everything:

- The *residual evaluation* `F(X)` is fully parallel over `t` — this is the "guess the whole trajectory and evaluate every step at once" part, and it is exactly why the idea is attractive.
- The *Jacobian* `J` of a one-step map is block lower-bidiagonal (step `t` couples only to `t-1`), so the Newton correction `J^{-1}F` is a forward substitution, i.e. *sequential in `T`* — unless it is attacked with cyclic reduction (see §2.6).

This is not a new idea; it is the **multiple shooting** method, and **Parareal** is a cheap-Jacobian approximation of it (details and sources in §2.1).

**What "forgets its past" means.** For deterministic dynamics, the sensitivity of `x_{t+s}` to `x_t` is the product of Jacobians, with magnitude growing like `e^{λs}` where `λ` is the maximal Lyapunov exponent. "Forgetting" means `λ < 0` (dissipative/contractive): a perturbation at time `t` is *damped*, not amplified, as it propagates forward. For MCMC, the analogous property is **mixing** — the distribution of `x_{t+s}` becomes independent of `x_t` — or, operationally, **regeneration**: times at which the chain's future is independent of its past. In both cases "forgets its past" = long-range causal coupling decays, so a bad guess early on is washed out by the time it matters.

## 1. Predictions (made before checking the literature)

- **P1.** The "guess + Newton-correct" proposal is real and studied: it is multiple shooting, with Parareal / MGRIT / PFASST as its practical realisations. It parallelises the *expensive* part (segment integration) while leaving a *cheap* sequential part (coarse propagation / bidiagonal Newton solve).
- **P2.** Fast convergence (`k ≪ T` iterations) requires the coarse-guess error to decay forward — i.e. the system must forget (negative Lyapunov exponents, dissipative, fast mixing). A memoryful or chaotic system should need `O(T)` iterations (no speedup) or diverge.
- **P3.** The linear case is the exception: `x_T = A^T x_0` is computable in `O(log T)` depth by repeated squaring/diagonalisation, with no forgetting assumption.
- **P4.** For a *single* daily rainfall-runoff run, compute is not the blocker — a forward run of a lumped conceptual model is trivially cheap; the real cost is calibration/uncertainty over *parameters*, which is embarrassingly parallel across parameters, not across time.
- **P5.** For a single long MCMC chain, the blocker is *mixing* (a statistical property), not FLOPs; GPUs add width (many chains, data-parallel likelihoods) but not depth (they don't shorten one chain's critical path), except via speculative prefetching, which is a branch-prediction trick with bounded speedup that is largest precisely when the chain barely moves.
- **P6.** "A shit ton of GPU parallelism" can reduce the cheap sequential part from `O(T)` to `O(log T)` via cyclic reduction, dropping per-iteration depth to `O(log T)`, but it cannot reduce the *number of iterations* `k`, which is set by the forgetting rate.

Predicted headline: the primary blocker is the system's memory/mixing, not compute — i.e. **NOT COMPUTE-BOUND** — with compute mattering only in specific subproblems.

## 2. Analysis

### 2.1 The method is real and well-understood

The proposal — guess the whole trajectory, then Newton-correct the continuity conditions — is literally **multiple shooting**. Wikipedia's statement of the method matches the question almost verbatim: partition the interval at grid points, "start by guessing the values of y at all grid points," integrate each sub-interval from its guessed initial value, and impose the matching conditions with "a modification of Newton's method" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_multiple_shooting_method).

The Gander–Vandewalle analysis of Parareal makes the connection explicit: multiple shooting is "to decompose the time-integration interval into subintervals, to solve an initial value problem on each subinterval concurrently, and to force continuity of the solution branches on successive intervals by means of a Newton procedure" (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/parareal.pdf). Parareal itself was introduced by Lions, Maday, and Turinici as a coarse/fine predictor-corrector in time (https://parallel-in-time.org/methods/parareal.html), and MGRIT (Falgout et al.) is the non-intrusive multigrid-reduction-in-time version shipped as XBraid (https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid; https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1184744).

### 2.2 The "forgets its past" condition is essentially the enabling condition

This is where P2 gets tested against the record.

- **Contractive/dissipative systems converge fast.** Gander and Hairer prove *superlinear* convergence of Parareal for nonlinear ODEs on bounded intervals — the error after iteration `k` is `O(ΔT^{p(k+1)})/(k+1)!`-style, shrinking as `k` grows (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/gander_plenary2007.pdf). For parabolic (dissipative) PDEs, MGRIT is demonstrated to be an optimal-scaling solver (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1184744), and LLNL reports time-to-solution drops of "tenfold or more" for compressible Navier-Stokes (https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).
- **Chaotic / non-forgetting systems fail or degenerate.** The same Gander–Hairer paper shows that on the Lorenz equations (chaotic), the superlinear convergence "stops at a certain level" as chaos amplifies the coarse-grid discrepancy. More bluntly, LLNL's report on chaotic problems states that for hyperbolic/chaotic problems "the most common method, parareal, diverging in many cases," because "chaotic initial value problems are inherently ill-conditioned" (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1880928), and Vargas et al. open with the same point: chaos makes subtle coarse-level inaccuracies explode into bad coarse-grid corrections (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441). This is exactly the "does not forget" failure mode: a positive Lyapunov exponent means a bad guess at time `t` is amplified forward, so the Newton/coarse correction never settles.

So, for nonlinear systems: yes, the value of the method tracks the forgetting rate. The method *is* a way to convert "sequential-in-time" into "parallel + iterate," and the iteration count `k` is governed by how fast errors decay — a property of the dynamics, not the hardware.

### 2.3 The exception: linear systems get parallel-in-time for free

For a linear map `x_{t+1} = A x_t`, the final state is `x_T = A^T x_0`, computable by repeated squaring in `O(log T)` depth. The "direct time parallel methods based on diagonalisation" (ParaDiag/ParaExp) exploit exactly this, solving the whole time interval at once for linear problems (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/siamtoc3.php, §5.5). No forgetting is needed — confirming P3 — because a linear propagator can be composed out of order. This is the only regime where the causality principle can be cleanly side-stepped.

### 2.4 The fundamental depth limit: causality and inherent sequentiality

Gander's survey names the obstacle plainly: for evolution problems "there is a causality principle: the solution later in time is affected (it is even determined) by the solution earlier in time, but not the other way round" (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/50YearsTimeParallel.pdf). That is not just folklore: in complexity theory, the forward simulation of a local dynamics is a canonical example of a *probably inherently sequential* problem. The P-completeness page lists "Game of Life — given an initial configuration ... is that cell alive after T steps" among the problems that are "probably not parallelizable" / "inherently sequential" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-complete), and Greenlaw–Hoover–Ruzzo's *Limits to Parallel Computation* develops the framework: such problems appear to lack polylog-time, polynomial-processor (NC) algorithms, i.e. "applying more processors ... appears to be broken" for them (https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~ruzzo/papers/limits.pdf).

The consequence: there is **no general free lunch**. For arbitrary local dynamics with memory, no number of processors removes the `O(T)` causal dependence. Parallel-in-time methods work only by *exploiting structure* — contraction (Parareal/MGRIT), linearity (ParaDiag), or a coarse/fine work separation that leaves a cheap serial residue.

### 2.5 The MCMC analog, and why Newton does not literally apply

A Metropolis-Hastings step is a stochastic accept/reject branch, not a smooth map, so there is no residual to Newton-solve. The faithful analog of "guess + correct" is **speculative prefetching**: speculatively evaluate many possible future states (the accept/reject tree) in parallel, keep the true path, discard the rest. Two recorded facts matter:

- Running many independent chains "does not change the mixing time for any single chain" (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf). So the embarrassingly-parallel answer does *not* reduce the sequential length that a slow-mixing chain needs.
- Prefetching's speedup is *bounded and constant-factor*, not a complexity win: naive prefetching gives `O(log2 J)` with `J` cores, and Byrd et al.'s "speculative moves" gives expected speedup `≈ 1/α` (about 4.3 at the optimal 0.234 acceptance rate) (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf; https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7265). Note the perverse structure: this speedup is largest when rejection dominates, i.e. when the chain is *barely moving* — the opposite of fast mixing.

The "forgets its past" condition for MCMC is **regeneration**. Mykland, Tierney, and Yu introduced splitting into MCMC samplers precisely so that the tours between regeneration times are i.i.d. and "allows Markov chain sampling to take advantage of a parallel computing environment without the problems created by many short Markov chain runs" (https://galton.uchicago.edu/~mykland/paperlinks/MyklandTierneyYu2291148.pdf). Coupling from the past (Propp & Wilson) parallelises the *other* way: run the chain from *all* possible states simultaneously under a monotone coupling, and coalescence certifies an exact sample — but this is efficient only when coalescence (≈ mixing) is fast (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/206-RWG/RWGpapers/propp_wilson.pdf). Both are literally "the system forgets" conditions.

This exposes the central tension, and it is the sharpest version of P2/P5:

> A single long chain is needed *only when* mixing is slow; but slow mixing is *exactly when* time-parallelism (regeneration, CFTP, prefetching) gives little or nothing.

If the chain mixes fast, you don't need one long chain — many short independent chains suffice, and that is embarrassingly parallel already. If it mixes slowly, the memory is what forces the long run, and that memory is what defeats time-parallel correction. So for MCMC, time-parallelism is largely self-defeating, consistent with the P-completeness intuition of §2.4.

### 2.6 Is compute a major blocker? The GPU question

**Width versus depth.** GPUs add enormous *width* (SIMD lanes), and modern samplers use it in two ways: running many chains at once, and data-parallel gradient/log-density evaluation *within* a single chain. TensorFlow Probability's HMC "gets parallelism both within-chain (mostly from data parallelism) and across chains ... for free" on GPUs/TPUs (https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2022/11/13/stan-and-tensorflow-for-fast-parallel-bayesian-inference/; https://export.arxiv.org/pdf/2002.01184). But width does not shorten the *depth* of a single trajectory: the critical path remains `T × (per-step cost) × (mixing overhead)`. This is the Amdahl's-law-in-time point.

**Where massive parallelism does buy depth.** The cheap sequential part of the PinT methods — the coarse propagation / block-bidiagonal Newton solve — is a (block) tridiagonal/bidiagonal solve. Parallel cyclic reduction (PCR) solves such a system in `O(log N)` steps using `N`-fold parallelism (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs554/fa2015/notes/09_tridiagonal_8up.pdf). So "a shit ton of GPUs" genuinely changes the per-iteration depth from `O(T)` to `O(log T)`, giving total depth `O(k log T)`. But `k` — the number of Parareal/MGRIT/Newton iterations — is set by the contraction rate, a property of the *dynamics*, not the hardware. GPUs buy the log factor and the constants; they do not buy `k`. This is P6 confirmed.

**The hydrology example confirms compute is not the time-dimension blocker.** A single daily-step rainfall-runoff forward run is cheap; the published compute burden in exactly this setting is Monte-Carlo parameter calibration and GLUE uncertainty analysis, parallelised with MPI/OpenMP/CUDA *across parameter sets* — embarrassingly parallel, and explicitly not across time steps (https://doi.org/10.3390/w15152810; https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/12/10/2667). If anything, the literature treats these as "internally concurrent" in the *parameter* direction, never the time direction — because there is nothing to gain in the time direction for a cheap lumped model.

### 2.7 Synthesis

The proposed scheme — guess the whole trajectory, Newton-correct every step at once — is a real, studied technique (multiple shooting → Parareal → MGRIT). For *nonlinear* systems it works well only when the coarse-guess error is damped forward, i.e. when the system **forgets** (dissipative/contractive, or regenerating/fast-mixing for MCMC); it fails or degenerates for long-memory and chaotic dynamics. Linear systems are the one exception where exact parallel-in-time is possible without forgetting. Compute is a *secondary* constraint: for a single rainfall-runoff run it is negligible; for MCMC the binding constraint is mixing, which GPUs do not fix (they add width, and via cyclic reduction they can shave the cheap sequential part of PinT from `O(T)` to `O(log T)`, but not the iteration count `k`). The primary determinant of whether time-parallelism works at all is the system's memory/mixing — a mathematical/stability property, not a compute property.

VERDICT: NOT COMPUTE-BOUND

# Related problems and where compute actually binds

Each heading names one concrete option from framer.md, with which part of the root question it bears on, whether more parallel compute changes its answer (open / settled / none), and the sequential structure of one answer.

## Multiple shooting

The root question's scheme verbatim: guess the trajectory at every grid point, integrate each sub-interval from its guessed value in parallel, then force continuity with a Newton iteration (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_multiple_shooting_method).

- **Root link:** Q1 — whether a single long sequential simulation can be parallelised over time by guessing the whole trajectory and Newton-correcting every step at once.
- **Compute:** none (convergence is set by the Newton iteration, not by how many processors evaluate segments).
- **Sequential:** one answer is one trajectory needing k Newton iterations, each a forward substitution in which interval t's correction waits on interval t-1 (O(m) deep for m intervals), while the m segment integrations are independent and parallelise exactly; the correction chain is the only serial residue because J is block lower-bidiagonal (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/parareal.pdf).

## Parareal

The cheap-Jacobian realisation of multiple shooting, introduced by Lions, Maday and Turinici: a coarse serial propagator predicts the trajectory and fine integrators correct each interval in parallel, iterating to convergence (https://parallel-in-time.org/methods/parareal.html).

- **Root link:** Q2 — whether the guess+Newton-correct trick only works when the system forgets its past — and Q1.
- **Compute:** none (the iteration count k is set by the forgetting rate, not the hardware).
- **Sequential:** each iteration marches a coarse propagator serially over all T subintervals (step t waits on t-1) while the T fine integrations are independent, so one run's depth is k·T, with k set by the forward decay of the coarse-guess error — Gander and Hairer show superlinear convergence only for contractive systems (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/gander_plenary2007.pdf).

## MGRIT

The non-intrusive multigrid-reduction-in-time version of Parareal (shipped as XBraid), which coarsens the time grid rather than using a separate coarse model (https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).

- **Root link:** Q3 — whether compute is a blocker and could be fixed with massive GPU parallelism.
- **Compute:** settled — for parabolic (dissipative) PDEs MGRIT is demonstrated to be an optimal-scaling solver, and LLNL reports "tenfold or more" time-to-solution drops for compressible Navier-Stokes, so more parallel compute already pays off there (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1184744; https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).
- **Sequential:** one run keeps the same coarse/fine structure as Parareal — a coarse-grid correction sweeps the time levels in order while fine-grid integrations are independent — and the iteration count is set by the contraction (forgetting) rate, not processor count, so the causal coarse sweep cannot be reordered without cyclic reduction (https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).

## ParaDiag / ParaExp

Direct time-parallel methods for linear dynamics: x_T = A^T x_0 is computed by diagonalisation or repeated squaring in O(log T) depth, giving exact parallel-in-time with no forgetting assumption (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/siamtoc3.php).

- **Root link:** Q2's exception — the one regime where the causality principle can be cleanly side-stepped — and Q1.
- **Compute:** none.
- **Sequential:** none — the T sequential steps already collapse because the propagator A^T can be composed out of order by repeated squaring/diagonalisation in O(log T) parallel steps (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/siamtoc3.php).

## Cyclic reduction (PCR)

Parallel cyclic reduction solves the block-bidiagonal Newton correction (a tridiagonal/bidiagonal system) in O(log N) steps with N-fold parallelism, dropping the per-iteration depth of the PinT methods from O(T) to O(log T) (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs554/fa2015/notes/09_tridiagonal_8up.pdf).

- **Root link:** Q3 — the "shit ton of GPU parallelism" question — specifically whether width can shorten the cheap sequential part.
- **Compute:** settled — N-fold parallel cyclic reduction is known to solve a tridiagonal system in O(log N) steps instead of O(N), so more parallel compute already buys the O(T)→O(log T) per-iteration depth reduction (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs554/fa2015/notes/09_tridiagonal_8up.pdf).
- **Sequential:** the block-bidiagonal solve is a forward substitution in which row t waits on row t-1 (O(T) deep per iteration), but the rows need not run in order: cyclic reduction eliminates independent pairs simultaneously, which pays off only when the T equations can be halved each round and the machine has ~T processors to feed them (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs554/fa2015/notes/09_tridiagonal_8up.pdf).

## Speculative prefetching

The MCMC analog of guess+correct: speculatively evaluate many possible accept/reject branches in parallel, keep the true path, discard the rest, with a speedup that is bounded and constant-factor (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf).

- **Root link:** Q2 for MCMC — whether the trick only works when the system forgets — and Q3's width-versus-depth point.
- **Compute:** none (mixing binds; prefetching only reduces latency with a bounded, constant-factor speedup).
- **Sequential:** one MH chain is a serial accept/reject sequence (each proposal waits on the previous accepted state, T steps per run), and prefetching speculates J future branches in parallel but keeps one path, giving O(log2 J) depth with J cores and expected speedup ≈1/α ≈ 4.3 at the 0.234 acceptance rate, largest when rejection dominates (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf; https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7265).

## Regeneration / splitting

Splitting an MCMC sampler at regeneration times yields i.i.d. tours that can be simulated in parallel, avoiding the bias of many short independent chains (https://galton.uchicago.edu/~mykland/paperlinks/MyklandTierneyYu2291148.pdf).

- **Root link:** Q2 for MCMC — regeneration is the operational "forgets its past" condition.
- **Compute:** none.
- **Sequential:** none — the tours between regeneration times are i.i.d. and already split into independent pieces that can run on separate processors, leaving only the mixing-governed length of one tour as the serial residue (https://galton.uchicago.edu/~mykland/paperlinks/MyklandTierneyYu2291148.pdf).

## Coupling from the past

Propp-Wilson exact sampling: run the chain from all possible states simultaneously under a monotone coupling, and coalescence certifies an exact draw, efficient only when coalescence (mixing) is fast (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/206-RWG/RWGpapers/propp_wilson.pdf).

- **Root link:** Q2 for MCMC — coalescence is the "forgets its past" condition.
- **Compute:** none.
- **Sequential:** none — the coupled chains run from all states in parallel under one monotone update, so the work already splits across states, and the only serial quantity is the coalescence time, which is set by mixing, not compute (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/206-RWG/RWGpapers/propp_wilson.pdf).

## Many-chain / data-parallel sampling (TFP HMC)

GPUs/TPUs add width two ways — many chains at once and data-parallel gradient/log-density evaluation within one chain — but width does not shorten a single chain's critical path (https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2022/11/13/stan-and-tensorflow-for-fast-parallel-bayesian-inference/).

- **Root link:** Q3 — the GPU question — specifically the width-versus-depth distinction.
- **Compute:** open — the quantity more parallel compute would buy is the number of independent chains/seeds analysed: Angelino et al. show running many chains "does not change the mixing time for any single chain" (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf), and no cited source establishes whether adding more chains/seeds above that changes the posterior estimate (e.g. finds additional modes).
- **Sequential:** none — many chains and within-chain data-parallel likelihoods are already independent pieces, so the answer already splits across GPUs, and the per-chain critical path (T × per-step cost × mixing overhead) is unchanged by width (https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2022/11/13/stan-and-tensorflow-for-fast-parallel-bayesian-inference/).

## GLUE / rainfall-runoff calibration

The actual compute burden in daily-step rainfall-runoff modelling is Monte-Carlo parameter calibration and GLUE uncertainty analysis, parallelised with MPI/OpenMP/CUDA across parameter sets, explicitly not across time steps (https://doi.org/10.3390/w15152810).

- **Root link:** Q3 — the hydrology example showing compute is not a time-dimension blocker.
- **Compute:** settled — the compute burden is parameter calibration/GLUE uncertainty, parallelised across parameter sets (embarrassingly parallel, never across time), so more parallel compute already buys parameter-set throughput, not time-step depth (https://doi.org/10.3390/w15152810; https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/12/10/2667).
- **Sequential:** none — each parameter set is one cheap forward run of a lumped model and parameter sets are independent, so the work already splits into independent pieces with no serial time chain to shorten (https://doi.org/10.3390/w15152810).

## Chaotic / non-forgetting PinT

On chaotic systems (Lorenz, hyperbolic PDEs) the coarse-guess error is amplified forward, so Parareal diverges or its superlinear convergence stops, because chaotic initial value problems are inherently ill-conditioned (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1880928; https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441).

- **Root link:** Q2 — whether the trick only works when the system forgets — here the non-forgetting failure mode.
- **Compute:** open — the quantity more parallel compute would buy is the coarse-grid resolution or number of processors fed to the coarse propagator: published results stop at divergence ("parareal diverging in many cases", https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1880928), and whether scaling coarse-grid fidelity or iteration count changes convergence above that is unresolved (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441).
- **Sequential:** the coarse propagator must march the time levels in order (step t waits on t-1), so one run's depth is T × k iterations, and the positive-Lyapunov amplification means the iterations cannot be collapsed by reordering the causal chain; the nearest attempt at a fix is the coarse-grid-correction study in (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441).
